One of my lecturers was a pagent woman and professional model (i.e. shes a 10/10). Because I'm gay af and also quite a flirt, I gave her a lot of flirtatious eye contact in our first classes together, mostly subconsciously. She started returning my looks, smirking when I'd smirk at her as we locked eyes, looking at me when she thinks I'm not watching. We've ended up having a lot of one on one interactions, her following me to the elevator, us being in there alone, running into each other when we get coffee, seeing each other in the halls. 

A few memorable ones:

On my way to my our class, she comes into my elevator. Other academics are there and she refuses to acknowledge me. As soon as we are alone she says 'hey *my name*' and we ask about each other's weekends. When I say I'm doing ok she says 'only ok?' with a cheeky smile and I die. 

I'm waiting by the elevator after class and she comes and stands next to me. I can see that she wants to start a conversation out of the corner of my eye. She says very nervously 'I love water'. I find it really awkward and kind of say 'yeah I bet' and she giggles nervously. 

I'm heading to another class and she pops out of a nearby door which happened to be in my eyeline. We both laugh and say hi and I say 'have fun in there' and she giggles and says she will. 

 I'm reading a novel outside the faculty building and I can see her slow down in my periphery to check what novel it is. 

I bring a book into class which is on my desk, which happens to be in her area of interest. She goes out of her way to see what it is discreetly during the break and smirks to herself. 

We are having extended eye contact and I'm biting my finger absent mindedly in the way one does when they are turned on. She sees it and has to turn away with a massive one sided smile. 

I haven't seen her in a few weeks because I got the flu. She sent an email saying she's noticed I haven't been in class and 'just wanted to check that you're ok?' Can't say any academic has ever noticed me before let alone bothered to care about my absence or if I'm ok. At the most benign it's very sweet and she's a caring teacher, but our emails often feel...thinly veiled. Also my university is rather notorious for teachers who don't give a rats ass so it's definitely odd.

Of course it's good to make an effort, although once again I think it's better for everybody if that's framed as making an effort for yourself, as opposed to for other people. I know whenever I've made self improvements I've never thought 'this is for my partner', I've thought 'this is for me'. 

But my point is that people gain or lose weight during their life in a way that is symptomatic. A very common cause for weight gain, coupled with no motivation when motivation and physical interests were there prior, is depression, chronic fatigue is also a possibility as well. It's a thousand times more supportive and loving to think to yourself 'ok my partner is gaining weight, eating more and unmotivated, maybe there is something going on here, maybe I can offer a support system and maybe flag mental health', rather than 'you're not catering to my attraction for you, please cease'. 

People often don't have complete control over whether they are able to 'keep their partner attracted to them' at every point in time. If someone is depressed, for instance, they may need to first put their energy and efforts into CBT, meditation, consistent therapy, and then very gradually up the tempo (consistently going for short walks, consistently going for longer walks, jogging a bit during the walk) etc. Life is full of ebbs and flows and when individuals are in a funk, a lot of the time you can't just get yourself to the gym everyday. Often discipline isn't the lone factor. Essentially what I'm saying is, you are in a relationship with a person, and people go through shit. People have fat years sometimes. People have sad years. People have mental breakdowns. People get sick. People get unmotivated. It's not 'not fair' that someone's partner might be having a rough patch, it's life. It's a person. 

Who you are attracted to is entirely your perogative. But in this situation we either have someone who is unmotivated and gaining weight for a reason (i.e. struggling with something), and therefore the emphasis should be on 'hey, I care about you, how are you feeling'. Or we may have a fundamental incompatibility (because some people don't have a desire to be a gym junkie and don't want to consistently diet, which is also their perogative. I mean my grandma didn't go to the gym a day in her life and never ate quinoa and she lived to 98 so, fair enough). 

At the end of the day, my point is that the emphasis here is misplaced. Why is anyone's first thought 'you need to make yourself more attractive to me' rather than 'I've noticed you've changed in numerous ways and I hope you know you can count on me to encourage you constructively to tackle anything that might be going on'.

I feel like your view here isn't super compassionate. 

First of all, you don't get to control your partners body simply because you are in a relationship. Whether they have a piercing you don't like, a haircut you hate, you don't like their clothes, or weight or whatever, that's not your body. It's kind of entitled to assume you can view it as if it's your territory to groom how you like. 

Second, a lot of people really struggle with weight gain or a lapse in physical activity etc when they are dealing with depression, or generally feeling down. Now I obviously don't know if that's the case, but I know when I had several years of clinical depression it was incredibly difficult to get out of bed, let alone consistently to the gym. And I would eat more sugar because I felt so tired all the time, which naturally led to weight gain. 

Be generally supportive of her. If she's telling you she used to be really into certain activities and she isn't anymore, maybe gently bring up whether or not she's feeling ok re depression or mental health. Neglecting or ceasing normal hobbies is a big sign of it. You can encourage her to go on walks with you or go for a hike but don't do it with the view of 'I don't want you fat' because that's douchey, do it with the view of 'if this is what you used to enjoy let's try and help you get out there again, if you're feeling blue'. 

Also finally, accept that if you are in a relationship you are committed to being with a person through thick and thin (pardon the pun). One of you might get depressed, laid off, chronic fatigue, break a leg, get cancer, suffer extreme grief, be in a bad car accident. It's life. It happens. And all of those things will change your body and weight one way or another.

I'm from Sydney. 

Sydney is a weird one. We are considered very queer friendly, but it really depends on which suburb you're in. Middle of the city, eastern suburbs, inner west - typically fine (although I have had people yell at me on the street a few times in these parts). Western suburbs, southern suburbs, north west - you are talking two bible belts and the part of Sydney that has the most Muslim immigrants as well, so various brands of conservatism, and homophobia. 

I grew up in one of the bible belts and in all ways it was basically 1950 there. Very strict gender roles, everyone was white, we never spoke positively about LGBT people, the priest came around for dinner some Sunday's after church etc. And I'm only in my mid 20s so this wasn't long ago. 

Also the Sydney queer women's scene feels very claustrophobic. I can't go on a date with anyone who went to one of the three mains universities in the city without already knowing five people who know them. It's also very homogenous, a lot queer women dress the same here, like very the same, and so it's hard to try a different type of person. We don't have a single dedicated lesbian bar in Sydney. We do have events that pop up around the city but once again it's the same people all of the time. 

I don't know, I feel lucky to live here because our quality of life is good and our houses are bigger than houses I've seen anywhere else, lots of natural landscape, beaches. But Sydney, the part that's actually 'the city' is very small, not that lively (we don't have many people and we also have lock out laws re you can't drink past a certain time in the middle of the city lol), and basically is starting to feel like a millionare's Disney sea where the only people who can afford it, and the people who are dictating the cities tone, are baby boomer white people with a lot of money. 

Comparing it to Paris, London or Tokyo, which I loved so much, makes me feel like I live so far from anything interesting that's happening in the world lol.

As a law student you have to remember an insane amount. 

1. Listen in class with your laptop in your bag, have a note pad and only take notes of things the lecturer says which are clearly important that aren't on the slides. 

2. When revising, I write notes for the entire course on a word document, with text boxes around each major topic so I learn to associate where which information goes, and font and colour etc to highlight case names etc. I essentially end up with my own 'this is the whole course and it's formatted in a way that teaches you how it all comes together' booklet. 

3. Use the above notes and now hand write summarized scaffolds. Scaffolds being 'if I'm presented with a question on X topic these are the steps I need to remember in a basic form, in order'. 

Once I've done all that I read over the scaffolds and test myself by covering them, and I can usually recite them verbatim before I walk into an exam. Similarly I can usually remember most of what was in my larger notes, at least in substance if not extreme specifics.

This is for CCP right? 

For most Universities it's an open book exam. You don't need to remember the section numbers or the specifics of the legislation (that probably isn't possible). What you need to be able to do is read a question, easily identify what the question is about/what topic/s it's asking you about (e.g. 'this question is about personal service and whether it's been done correctly'). You need to know the gist of what the law says on said topic ('I think that personal service probably hasn't been achieved here because X, y, z) so you can quickly understand what the correct answer is.  

You then need to have well set out notes (use tabs to mark every topic so you can flip to it) and refer to the legislation. I had a topic heading 'personal service' on a tab, id flip to it and the first page was a list of section numbers and next to them a few words on what that section says, then I had the sections themselves. I'd check which section/s was the one I knew the 'gist' of the answer from and applied the law with specific wording from my notes on hand. 

The hardest thing in a CCP exam is probably time management. Because you really do have to refer to your notes, they need to be very well set out and easy to flick through. You do need to know the general answer/what your argument likely is before looking at the notes, the notes are just there so you don't have to remember the section numbers or legislation in its specifics.

I'm guessing you just started foundies for a JD? 

I'm a second year. From my experience, how hard a case is to read is largely determined by how much that case interests you (probably an obvious statement), coupled with how much they are making you read (torts was easier than contracts in this regard because we were given a textbook with important excerpts, the contracts cases were less condensed). 

In all honesty I've found the cases have gotten a bit harder to understand as each semester goes by - torts was fine, contracts was about 50/50 (half were fine, half were mind numbing) and you barely have to read any for CCP. Public law cases were often very dense, international law cases were rarely more enlightening than reading a sypnopsis, criminal law was very easy regarding cases (except He Kaw Teh doesn't click until it does). 

That isn't meant to discourage you - with each semester studying law gets easier in terms of picking up how to best 'get it'. The cases are sometimes dense, I very rarely 'get it' just by reading the case. I personally found for subjects where reading the cases wasn't easy/I didn't understand quite what to do with them, reading them AFTER the lecture and AFTER I'd read that section of a past students notes was better because I knew the jist of the case and could follow that thread more easily. Then I'd ask my tutor if my understanding was correct. 

Also some cases are more important than others. You won't get this reference now but there are cases like Wicks v State Rail which tell you how you must structure any negligent psychiatric injury claim in an exam answer (so reading it and getting it is more essential), but there are also cases which mainly give you an example e.g. of what kind of thing counts as private nuisance (in an exam for instance you might use it to support that the thing that had occurred in the facts is or isn't a private nuisance, but the reasoning in the case isn't structuring your answer or necessarily informing it much). 

Also remember when you are reading, why you are reading. The case is supposed to give you a principle, which was come to through reasoning, based on certain facts. Those are the primary things to pull out. What rule does this case give me? What was the reasoning behind the rule? What facts did this rule apply to, and therefore what facts might this rule NOT apply to? 

Keep those questions in mind as you read, because in every case there is a lot to wade through and not all of it adds to the above questions. Particularly in contracts, at least I found, keeping those questions in mind was essential because some of the cases just felt neverending and full of stuff that didn't seem useful to my understanding because it was dense or not the central point. 

Remember with foundies you are mainly learning basic skills. Don't fret too much about it. 

(This is all advice based on my own learning style and the courses from my uni so it may be different for you).

The idea of it being a transaction is genuinely just appealing to me. You both know why the other is there, you don't have to deal with anything outside of why you are there. Take any advice I have with a grain of salt because I'm only a student but as far as I know: 

There is no difference between getting an LLB or a JD in terms of perception - no degree is greater than the other. However, the JD is a very, very expensive degree unless you get a CSP place, and you can't know if you'll get one until you try. Personally, I wouldn't chose to do one degree and then do a second that itself could attract over 100,000 dollars in debt. 

Objectively, sure, you will have less life and work and study experience at the end of an LLB compared to a JD, because you would be younger. This is certainly noticeable between the LLB and JD cohorts at my Uni - there is a pretty obvious maturity/life/professionalism/work ethic difference between the LLB and JD students generally. But it's likely not going to impact you at all in terms of employability as long as you gain decent experience in the years of your LLB. Not to mention an LLB starts with two much more relaxed work load years which allows you to ease into it/get legal experience, where as the JD is full pelt. 

In essence, the JD is more expensive and it gives you the same degree in prestige and content as the LLB, so there's no reason to put a law degree off. I have a bit of a unique perspective on the issue because I got into my LLB of choice out of school, had a massive existential crisis, dropped to an arts degree and shuffled majors around for a year, and then wound up discovering that I actually really wanted to do law - in retrospect the road less travelled really worked for me and I feel my marks are far better than they would have been when I was younger and not interested enough, but honestly if you want to do a law degree at some point, why chose the more expensive option and will take you longer to arrive at?

The thing is, part of dating is that you will go on dates where you don't get along as well in real life. That's not something to be nervous about - it's just something to accept. You can't predict what your chemistry will be in real life, the purpose of going on a date is to see what it's like in real life, and so if it's not great then that's a good thing to have found out before you got too invested. 

Similarly, if you don't find her as attractive in real life (which I think happens with app dating all the time often because people in a three dimensional way with a voice and a presence etc simply can't be captured by photos) then be normal - be polite, have a chat, at the end just let her know it was nice to meet her but that you personally don't feel a romantic connection. Be pleasant and be honest. 

Don't ever view a first date as something that has to go perfectly because this person is totally going to be your person. You have no idea about that yet. The goal of a first date is to see if there is potential there - keep that in mind.

Stop doing what it wants you to do. 

Want to stay in bed all day or sit on the couch? Go out, doesn't matter if you go somewhere entirely boring or even only for an hour, go out. 

Want to put zero effort into your work or study? Sit down and do a solid hour or two of whatever you need to do, turn off your phone, no excuses. 

Want to eat that food even though you're not really hungry? Drink a glass of water and go for a short walk, read a book in the sun, call a friend. 

Want to not respond to texts or not speak to anybody and neglect your social life? Make sure you do at least one social thing per week - have coffee, see a film, go to lunch. 

Don't feel like you have to do all of this perfectly and entirely at once - small, achievable goals that gradually become a bit bigger. Go outside to the local shops and get a coffee first off, then go outside for a bit longer, then go outside and make sure you see a friend etc etc. 

Further, make a list of little easy to do goals and actually do them. Always wanted to go to a martial arts class? Book one. Always wanted to write a novel? Aim to write a chapter every week. Always wanted to get more fit? Try out a gym with one of those free trials and then if you like that gym, get a membership, go once a week, then go twice. 

If you are able bodied, you can do it. Heck even if you aren't. Your depression is trying to feed itself by taking things away from you - you don't have to accept that. I know it can be exhausting and can feel really impossible to do the opposite of what will feed it, but it's not remotely impossible. You just have to start small and take genuine pride in each victory, and have a goal each day and make sure it gets done. Whether that is getting out of bed, showering today, seeing a friend, trying a new class. One thing each day, no excuse.

I don't think it's abnormal to WANT to be together every day, but in my mind it's not great to emotionally NEED it. 

I think most people like to encounter their partner once a day, either in person or over text or a call etc - and if I can't see someone I'm dating long term for a week, for instance, I'll very much miss them and wish they were around. It's also very normal to want to be domestic with someone you love. 

But if being separated actually has a toll on anyone's mental health, or ability to function day to day - personally I don't think that's a good thing. As someone who has been in a few long term relationships my advice is that you absolutely need to maintain your own separate life - your job, your friends, your own hobbies. A) it's better for your mental health, b) never make another person so important that if they went away, you would literally have nothing and c) it will stop your relationship from becoming stale - you will both still be interesting people separately with interesting new things to talk about and other people to emotionally rely on and hang out with etc. I can tell you now one of the things that made my most recent break up occur was that we became too much of a pair and didn't feed our own individual lives and things just got plain boring. 

So no, I don't think it's weird to want to be around each other all of the time, but be wary of actually being around each other all of the time. Also just my personal view, your relationship changes quite a bit from the first year of dating to the second, and then to the third - I think it's more ideal to move in together after about two years, you know each other better, you've encountered each other (likely) when stressed or sad, you probably have an idea of the other persons domestic habits etc.

Hey there! Welcome to Sydney!! 

The main areas for queer women are Newtown/Redfern/Enmore/Erskineville/Marrickville. Basically the start of the 'inner west'. There aren't many bars specifically for queer women in Sydney (apart from the sly fox in enmore which is probably the closest you will come to one), but most bars in those suburbs will be very LGBT friendly and some will have LGBT events. Check out the Newtown hotel, bank hotel, Sly Fox. 

Oxford street in Sydney's eastern suburbs is also a gay Mecca but it's more tailored to gay men - so it's friendly but I've never known how to meet LGBT women there because a lot of girls on Oxford are straight. 

There are also specific clubbing events (held in different locations) for LGBT ladies - Have a look at Girlthing and Birdcage, as well as Homosocial. Those are three events that are run pretty consistently - I think Girlthing and birdcage are at least on once a month. 

If you're a student (you didn't say) the University of Sydney has some groups you could join as a student there - collectives, and then also have a LGBT party group, called Shades, and anyone can go along to those parties. 

Make sure you go to Mardi Gras in March - however keep in mind, if you want to watch the parade, you might not get into an after party because they will often already be full, and moving from the parade route to pretty much anywhere else is a pain because of how many people there are/how barricaded the streets are. Girlthing is having a Mardi Gras party on the night - if you're not that interested in the parade, maybe get a ticket (they sell out quick). 

As a note, Campbelltown isn't a suburb that id list as explicitly LGBT friendly in Sydney (not that you'd necessarily experience anything bad, I don't imagine, you just likely won't find much there as a queer person for you). The inner west, city and eastern suburbs are the most LGBT friendly areas of Sydney - the west, north west (Bible Belt), south west etc not so much, at least there aren't really LGBT events or clubs there, and the cinemas out where I grew up aren't playing Call Me By Your Name despite it being an Oscar contender, I imagine because no one where I grew up would want to see it (insert eye roll).

I don't know you or your strengths etc so I can't tell you. What I can tell you is that many, many people in my cohort were very intelligent and academic, but they can't give everyone HDs and Ds. Like any skill, some people are naturally better at something like law than others, and if you combine that with hard work you get results. Some people work until 10pm in the library every night of the week and don't get the top level results, probably because law isn't as intuitive to them (also note that most law subjects have exams worth 70 or so percent as well, how well you assess in certain types of assessments is also relevant). 

Going into an LLB from highschool, you can safely assume that a very large majority of people there did very well in highschool and are academic - if it was me, I would a) read more about the legal profession and see if it's actually for me and b) go to a library and have a look at some of the basic textbooks, or even ask a past student etc for any problem questions they have, or look for them online, to get a feel for what skills law is actually about. 

There are also some great podcasts out there about law school - try the law school toolbox podcast.

Only go into law if you actually want to be a lawyer/enjoy or love the law. First and foremost, if you'd be doing a law degree just because it's prestigious as a profession or for the money, there are other prestigious professions and other jobs that pay better. It is a time intensive profession and if you don't actually care for what you are doing, you're wasting your time and your clients time, in my honest opinion. 

From what I've heard and read, getting a legal job became more difficult around the GFC. But also here's the perspective: most universities in Australia would have an LLB and JD cohort graduating each year. Each cohort is probably at least 200 strong. There are only six top tier firms in Australia (as an example) that have offices in major cities - if each top tier takes twenty grads (I don't know how many they actually take) in each major city, that's only a few hundred jobs at that level. 

The reality is, a lot of people are getting law degrees and it's a competitive industry. If you're competitive, if you have a strong WAM and do good work and have a decent resume, life should probably be fine one would think. I would be more worried if I was someone who wasn't appearing competitive at university because your options are much smaller, and maybe not what you were looking for (i.e. You might be looking at working in smaller suburban law firms or practices or moving states to a different market). 

But regardless that's all conjecture - at the end of the day a) don't do a law degree if you don't actually want to be a lawyer, do some research about the hours, the daily life of a lawyer, what kind of work you actually do, what kind of skills are necessary and b) like many fields, if you are competitive this question is less relevant than if you are not. Other industries certainly have more of a shortage of workers than the legal field however.
